You are an independent classifier in a blinded experiment about a book of
biblical symbolism. The consensus responses below were produced without access
to the book. Compare them with the book's entry.

TERM
Iron

BLIND CONSENSUS RESPONSES
RESPONSE A
{
  "primary_meaning": "Iron most commonly symbolizes strength, hardness, and unyielding power — especially severe, inflexible rule or judgment. The best-known expression is the messianic 'rod of iron,' denoting Christ's absolute, unbreakable authority over the nations, and more broadly iron connotes irresistible force, harshness, and severity (of rule, oppression, or affliction).",
  "primary_basis": [
    "Psalm 2:9 (he shall break them with a rod of iron)",
    "Revelation 2:26-27 (rule the nations with a rod of iron)",
    "Revelation 12:5 and 19:15 (the child/rider who rules with a rod of iron)",
    "Daniel 2:33, 40-43 (the fourth kingdom strong as iron that breaks and crushes all)",
    "Deuteronomy 28:48 (a yoke of iron upon your neck — oppressive subjugation)",
    "Jeremiah 28:13-14 (yoke of iron symbolizing Babylonian domination)"
  ],
  "alternatives": [
    {
      "meaning": "Affliction, bondage, and testing — the 'iron furnace' of Egypt as a symbol of harsh servitude from which God redeems his people.",
      "basis": [
        "Deuteronomy 4:20",
        "1 Kings 8:51",
        "Jeremiah 11:4",
        "Psalm 105:18 (his soul came into iron / laid in irons)"
      ],
      "prominence": "common"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "The fourth world empire (traditionally identified as Rome) in Daniel's statue vision — iron legs representing a crushing, militarily dominant kingdom.",
      "basis": [
        "Daniel 2:33, 40-43",
        "Daniel 7:7, 19 (beast with great iron teeth)"
      ],
      "prominence": "common"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "Mutual sharpening and edification between believers — 'iron sharpens iron.'",
      "basis": [
        "Proverbs 27:17"
      ],
      "prominence": "common"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "Human obstinacy and hardness of heart — a stiff, unbending neck or a hardened, seared conscience.",
      "basis": [
        "Isaiah 48:4 (your neck is an iron sinew)",
        "Jeremiah 6:28 (bronze and iron, all of them corrupt)",
        "1 Timothy 4:2 (conscience seared as with a hot iron)"
      ],
      "prominence": "minority"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "Human military might and worldly technological power set against God's people (sometimes extended homiletically to reliance on human strength).",
      "basis": [
        "Judges 1:19 and 4:3 (chariots of iron)",
        "Joshua 17:16-18",
        "1 Samuel 13:19-22 (Philistine iron monopoly)"
      ],
      "prominence": "minority"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "That which is common or base in contrast to precious metals — a symbol of inferiority or degradation (e.g., silver becoming dross, iron instead of silver).",
      "basis": [
        "Isaiah 60:17 (instead of iron I will bring silver)",
        "Jeremiah 6:28-30 (refining imagery)",
        "Ezekiel 22:18-20 (Israel as dross — bronze, tin, iron, lead in the furnace)"
      ],
      "prominence": "rare"
    }
  ],
  "has_settled_consensus": true,
  "confidence": "high",
  "notes": "Iron is a multivalent biblical image, but there is broad, recognizable agreement across commentaries, Bible dictionaries (e.g., entries on metals and on the rod of iron), and homiletic tradition that its core symbolic register is strength/hardness/severity — applied positively to Christ's unbreakable messianic rule (Psalm 2; Revelation) and negatively to oppressive kingdoms and yokes (Daniel 2; Deuteronomy 28; Jeremiah 28). Secondary uses (iron furnace as affliction, iron sharpening iron as edification) are context-specific rather than competing definitions. The 'rod of iron' itself has an internal interpretive debate (rule/shepherd vs. shatter, reflecting LXX 'poimaneis'), but both readings still treat iron as denoting inflexible strength."
}

  "has_settled_consensus": false,
  "confidence": "high",
  "notes": "Iron has no single settled biblical symbolic meaning independent of context. The broadest recognizable association is strength and hardness, but the same physical qualities support several related applications: irresistible rule, judgment, oppression, resilience, and stubbornness. Many biblical occurrences are also literal references to the metal rather than symbols."

BOOK ENTRY
The crushing strength of Daniel's fourth kingdom, historically identified here as Rome — the empire ruling when Christ came.

(none)

AVAILABLE KJV EXCERPTS
Daniel 2:40 — And the fourth kingdom shall be strong as iron: forasmuch as iron breaketh in pieces and subdueth all things: and as iron that breaketh all these, shall it break in pieces and bruise.
Daniel 8:20 — The ram which thou sawest having two horns are the kings of Media and Persia.
Daniel 8:21 — And the rough goat is the king of Grecia: and the great horn that is between his eyes is the first king.

CLASSIFY THE RELATIONSHIP

First reduce both readings to their minimum core identifications. Do not let
extra detail create an artificial disagreement.

- MATCH: the core identifications are equivalent. Differences are merely
  wording or immaterial detail.
- REFINED: the book preserves the consensus's general referent or category but
  materially changes its extension, boundary, conditions, or precision. A
  narrowing may reject some cases the broader consensus admits; a broadening
  may admit cases it excludes. This is real disagreement at the boundary, but
  not replacement of the central referent.
- DIVERGENT: the cores materially contradict. Both claims cannot be true of the
  same referent in the same context and sense; accepting the book requires
  rejecting or replacing the consensus identification. A source and its
  product remain different referents when the book explicitly denies their
  identity, even if they are causally related.
- NOVEL: no recognizable consensus or listed alternative covers the book's
  core identification. Novelty is absence from consensus, not contradiction.

Use `core_relation` to expose the relationship at the center and
`extension_relation` to expose disagreement over the cases covered. A REFINED
verdict must state what cases the book adds, excludes, or reclassifies. A
DIVERGENT verdict must identify a replaced referent or material contradiction,
not merely a narrower boundary.

Treat the two axes independently. A core-divergent reading may still retain
some cases covered by the consensus while rejecting its central identification;
therefore DIVERGENT does not require disjoint extensions. Conversely, a
narrowed extension is REFINED only when the consensus's central referent or
category remains intact.

Also judge whether the citations printed with the glossary entry alone provide
strong, partial, or insufficient support. Do not yet decide whether a divergent
full chapter is persuasive; that is a separate stage.
